solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Saxophonist’s case holds long instrument (6)

indicators.note: a word's case is its outside, so only the first and last letters of SAXOPHONIST are kept
the outer letters hold the next piece inside them

blocks.note: the outer letters of SAXOPHONIST
to pine is to long for

annotation.surface: A jazz musician's instrument case turns out to have something long packed inside it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective describing the instrument; it is the verb, to long or PINE. A spinet is a small harpsichord, nothing to do with saxophones.
annotation.definitionFit: A spinet is a small keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.

entries.clue: Perturbed at first, I ignore naughty lingerie (8)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of 'Perturbed'
the letters of I IGNORE misbehave, landing out of order

blocks.note: first letter of Perturbed
I IGNORE rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone flustered at first but then choosing to overlook some racy underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' seems to describe the lingerie, but it is the instruction to rearrange I IGNORE.
annotation.definitionFit: A peignoir is a light, loose dressing gown or negligee worn by women.

entries.clue: Bird originally nested under r*.oof (8)

indicators.note: take the words at their origin: the first letter of each of 'nested' and 'under'

blocks.note: first letters of Nested and Under
the clue word is 'roof', garbled in the scraped text; a thatch is a roof of straw

annotation.surface: A bird has made its nest in the eaves, tucked beneath the roof.
annotation.walkthrough: 'r*.oof' is the word 'roof' mangled when the clue was copied. 'Originally' covers both 'nested' and 'under'; the bird then sits under its THATCH, which in a down clue is simply written after.
annotation.definitionFit: The nuthatch is a small woodland bird that climbs trees headfirst.

entries.clue: Clement Attlee regularly supporting constitution (9)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: A, T, E from ATTLEE
in a down clue the supporter sits underneath, so ATE comes after TEMPER

blocks.note: a person's temper is their constitution or temperament
the 1st, 3rd and 5th letters of ATTLEE

annotation.surface: Clement Attlee, the post-war British prime minister, backing the constitution.
annotation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was Labour prime minister 1945 to 1951, so 'Clement' reads as his first name; it is the definition, meaning mild.
annotation.definitionFit: Clement weather or a clement climate is mild, the same as temperate.

entries.clue: Contemplate statisticians surrounded by booze (8)

indicators.note: the statisticians go inside the booze

blocks.note: cider, an alcoholic drink, wrapped around the next piece
the Office for National Statistics, the UK's statistics agency

annotation.surface: Number-crunchers ponder things while sitting in a sea of drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The ONS is the Office for National Statistics, the British government's statistics body.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean turning something over in the mind before deciding.

entries.clue: Ken crawled along rocks for it (6,9)

indicators.note: the letters are rocked and shaken about

blocks.note: KEN CRAWLED ALONG rearranged, 15 letters

annotation.surface: Ken has scrambled across some rocks to reach something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' is a common euphemism for sex, so the whole answer can be defined by that tiny word; 'rocks' reads as boulders but is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: 'It' as in 'doing it' means sex, and carnal knowledge is the old legal term for sexual intercourse.

entries.clue: Wise chief exchanging pounds for power (7)

indicators.note: swap one letter for another
gives the direction of the swap: the pounds go, the power comes in

blocks.note: the salient point is the chief one
L, from the Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pounds; it is removed
P is the symbol for power; it replaces the L

annotation.surface: A sage leader trading money for influence.
annotation.walkthrough: SALIENT becomes SAPIENT when its L (pounds) is swapped for P (power).
annotation.definitionFit: Sapient means wise, as in Homo sapiens, the wise human.

entries.clue: Thriller writer’s novel The Dingo (8)

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: THE DINGO rearranged

annotation.surface: A crime author's latest book is titled The Dingo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, fitting the thriller writer; it is the adjective meaning new. The 's stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: Len Deighton is the British author of spy thrillers such as The IPCRESS File.

entries.clue: State of royals is good, in truth (8)

indicators.note: 'In' in its sense of 'inside': the letter for good is placed in the middle of the word for truth

blocks.note: reality is truth, opened up to take the next letter
G is the standard abbreviation for good

annotation.surface: A statement that the monarchy is in good shape, honestly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State of royals' reads as an opinion on their health; it means the condition of being royal.
annotation.definitionFit: Regality is royalty, the state or quality of being regal.

entries.clue: Somebody’s grandfather clock? (3-5)

blocks.note: the surface asks whose clock it is, but a somebody is also a person of importance, a big shot
a tall longcase clock; taken literally, a large device for keeping time, and the question mark flags that literal reading

annotation.surface: Asking about the tall clock belonging to a notable person.
annotation.walkthrough: A somebody, an important person, is a BIG-TIMER; a grandfather clock, read literally, is a big timer, so the clock is what a somebody would be called.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: a big-timer has made it big, the opposite of a small-timer, which is what calling someone a somebody means.

entries.clue: Water jump(6)

blocks.note: a natural source where water wells up from underground
to leap suddenly upwards or forwards

annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a water jump in showjumping or steeplechase; split it into two separate meanings.
annotation.definitionFit: Spring water flows from the ground; spring as a verb means leap.

entries.clue: Secretly, Brahms and Liszt are manic (2,6)

indicators.note: rhyming slang for pissed, i.e. drunk: the letters stagger about

blocks.note: ARE MANIC rearranged

annotation.surface: A remark that two Romantic composers were privately rather frenzied.
annotation.walkthrough: Brahms and Liszt is British rhyming slang for pissed, meaning drunk, so the composers are the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: In camera, a legal term, means in private, away from public view.

entries.clue: Killing time with prince on isle, half-cut (6)

indicators.note: puts time and prince together
in an across clue, the first pair is placed on (after) the isle piece
cut the word in half and keep one half

blocks.note: the second half of ISLE
T is the abbreviation for time
Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare

annotation.surface: Someone passing the hours with royalty on an island, getting half-cut.
annotation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, a false trail; here it cuts ISLE in half. Hal is the name used for the young Prince Henry in Shakespeare's Henry IV.
annotation.definitionFit: Killing as an adjective, like a killing blow, means lethal.

entries.clue: Cocaine, cannabis and fruitcake (8)

blocks.note: crack is a form of cocaine
pot is slang for cannabis

annotation.surface: A list of drugs followed by an unexpected cake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fruitcake' reads as a third item on the shopping list; it is the slang for a mad person.
annotation.definitionFit: A fruitcake, in slang, is an eccentric or crazy person, a crackpot.

entries.clue: Alarmingly hard-left sermon containing common sense (9)

indicators.note: H (hard) has left, so it drops from HOMILY
what is left of the sermon holds common sense

blocks.note: HOMILY, a sermon, without H for hard
nous is British slang for common sense

annotation.surface: A frightening, politically extreme speech from the pulpit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hard-left' reads as the far left of politics; split it as H (hard) having left the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Ominously means in a threatening, alarming manner.

entries.clue: Part of fingerprint found in Star Chamber (4)

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the words that follow

blocks.note: stARCHamber

annotation.surface: Evidence turning up at the Star Chamber, the notorious old English court.
annotation.walkthrough: The Star Chamber was an English court of Tudor and Stuart times, famous for arbitrary judgments.
annotation.definitionFit: Fingerprints are classed by their patterns: arches, loops and whorls.

entries.clue: American doctor picked up more fresh, delicious food (8)

indicators.note: picked up by the ear, i.e. heard

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
rosier, with fresher, pinker cheeks, said in a non-rhotic British accent

annotation.surface: An American doctor has acquired some better-tasting fare.
annotation.walkthrough: In British speech the final R of ROSIER is silent, so it is heard as ROSIA.
annotation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the Greek gods, hence anything delicious.

entries.clue: Nickname of international banker caught in scam (8)

indicators.note: the banker is trapped inside the scam

blocks.note: a con is a scam
the gnomes of Zurich, a nickname for Swiss international bankers

annotation.surface: A notorious financier's alias is revealed when he is caught in a fraud.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The gnomes of Zurich' was a British politician's jibe at Swiss bankers, so a gnome is an international banker.
annotation.definitionFit: A cognomen is a nickname or surname; in Rome, the third name of a citizen.

entries.clue: Diplomat devoid of love and desire (4)

indicators.note: the diplomat is emptied of the love letter

blocks.note: an envoy is a diplomat sent on a mission
love is O, a zero score in tennis; it is removed

annotation.surface: A cold, loveless diplomat who is also without desire.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface lists two things the diplomat lacks, but 'and' joins the wordplay to the definition 'desire'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to covet what someone else has.

entries.clue: Found naked, lying around with artist and the like (2,6)

indicators.note: stripped of its outer letters
turned around so it reads backwards, going up the grid
'With' in its sense of 'together with': the artist is placed alongside, after the reversed piece

blocks.note: DETECTED (found) without its first and last letters
ETECTE reversed
RA, a Royal Academician, stands for an artist

annotation.surface: Someone discovered unclothed, sprawled out with a painter and others of that kind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Found' is not the finding of a body but the synonym DETECTED; strip and reverse it.
annotation.definitionFit: Et cetera means 'and the rest', or 'and the like'.

entries.clue: Extremely virile tough guys, tense and passionate (8)

indicators.note: take the extremes, first and last letters, of 'virile'

blocks.note: first and last letters of VIRILE
he-men are macho tough guys
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

annotation.surface: Describing a group of intensely macho men, all tense and fiery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'virile'; it takes that word's extremes.
annotation.definitionFit: Vehement means showing strong, passionate feeling.

entries.clue: Epicurean academic stopping robbery (8)

indicators.note: the academic plugs the gap in the robbery, going inside it

blocks.note: a heist is a robbery
a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

annotation.surface: A pleasure-loving professor intervenes to foil a raid.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Epicurean' could be an adjective, but it works as a noun here for the pleasure-seeker.
annotation.definitionFit: An Epicurean, after the Greek philosopher Epicurus, is a devotee of pleasure, a hedonist.

entries.clue: Hesitant husband becoming leader in Icelandic parliament (7)

indicators.note: the H moves to the front, taking the lead position

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband; it goes first
the ALTHING with its H taken out, to go up front

annotation.surface: A nervous man is elected to lead Iceland's legislature.
annotation.walkthrough: The Althing is Iceland's parliament; its H (husband) moves from the middle to the front, turning ALTHING into HALTING.
annotation.definitionFit: Halting speech is hesitant, stopping and starting.

entries.clue: Start to roll joint and cause annoyance (6)

indicators.note: take the start, the first letter, of 'roll'

blocks.note: first letter of ROLL
the ankle is a joint of the body

annotation.surface: Rolling a spliff and irritating someone.
annotation.walkthrough: After the drugs of 13 across, 'roll joint' reads as rolling a cannabis cigarette; the joint is the ankle.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that rankles causes lasting annoyance or resentment.

entries.clue: Grown weaker, ladies perhaps need exercises (8)

indicators.note: the letters of NEED are exercised, worked about into a new order

blocks.note: the ladies is a women's toilet, and toilets are loos; 'perhaps' marks the example
NEED rearranged

annotation.surface: Having gone weak, some women perhaps require a workout.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the ladies' is the women's public toilet, and loo is everyday British for toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: Something loosened has become slacker, its grip grown weaker.

entries.clue: Conference match bringing in two thousand (6)

indicators.note: the match takes the thousands inside it

blocks.note: to suit is to match
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so two of them

annotation.surface: A league fixture that pulls in a crowd of two thousand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conference' and 'match' suggest a sports league; 'match' is the verb SUIT.
annotation.definitionFit: A summit is a conference between heads of government.

entries.clue: Split always follows scorn (8)

indicators.note: the 'always' piece comes after the 'scorn' piece

blocks.note: to diss is to scorn, show disrespect
ever means always

annotation.surface: A statement that division always comes after contempt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Follows' fixes the order: the word for always comes after the word for scorn. Diss is modern slang, short for disrespect.
annotation.definitionFit: A rare, formal verb: the DIS- prefix intensifies SEVER, so it means to cut apart, or split.

entries.clue: Peter out smuggling dope back in refuse (8)

indicators.note: the dope is carried hidden inside
the dope is written backwards

blocks.note: to abate is to peter out, diminish
GEN, slang for information or dope, reversed

annotation.surface: Peter, a smuggler, sneaking drugs back into a rubbish dump.
annotation.walkthrough: Peter reads as a man's name and dope as drugs, and 'refuse' as rubbish. 'Dope' is information, GEN in British slang.
annotation.definitionFit: To abnegate is to renounce or refuse something, especially a right or pleasure.

entries.clue: Frivolous people voting for vacuous treaty (6)

indicators.note: empty: the middle of TREATY is removed, leaving its outer letters

blocks.note: yeas are the votes, or voters, in favour
first and last letters of TREATY

annotation.surface: Lightweight politicians backing an empty-headed agreement.
annotation.walkthrough: Yeas are the ayes in a vote; 'people voting for' gives those in favour.
annotation.definitionFit: Yeasty can mean frothy and trivial, like the foam on fermenting liquid.
